ai_profile.summary: This paper evaluates a passive DNS monitoring approach that clusters NXDOMAIN responses using lexical and temporal properties to detect Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) botnet activity before domains are registered. The methodology involved analyzing 30 days of query logs from three enterprise resolvers, scoring candidate domains with n-gram entropy and digit ratio, and training a random forest classifier on labeled DGA families like Conficker and Necurs. Results showed the system achieved 91.4% precision and 88.7% recall, detecting DGA bursts with a median latency of 42 minutes ahead of successful command-and-control registrations.

title: Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse

research_understanding.title: Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse
research_understanding.domain: Cybersecurity / Network Traffic Analysis / Threat Detection
research_understanding.dataset: 51 packet captures: 3 baselines (OS/browser), 24 normal control runs (6 automated browser tests per service across Discord, Dropbox, Gmail, OneNote), and 24 framework test runs (6 tests per framework across DaaC2, DBC2, gdog, Callidus).
research_understanding.results: Reputation detection completely failed (0% detection of C2 channels). Beacon detection with CV failed entirely (0/4), while K-means + DBSCAN clustering achieved 2/4 (detected gdog and DBC2, missed Callidus and DaaC2). JA4 TLS fingerprinting achieved 100% detection (24/24) with 0% false positives. Upload/download ratio achieved 100% detection (24/24) with 4% false positives (+96pp margin). The proof-of-concept Zeek real-time detector achieved 24/24 high-confidence detections on C2 runs with 0 high-confidence alerts on benign runs.
research_understanding.abstract: The ever-increasing adoption of trusted services and their interconnectivity with private resources provides new opportunities for malicious communication channels. Traditional indicators of compromise, such as IP/Domain reputation or beacon detection, are most effective against adversary-owned infrastructure but yield limited signals when communication channels run atop trusted services. This study contrasts normal user traffic with known malicious activity to identify alternative indicators from four public C2 frameworks (DaaC2, DBC2, gdog, Callidus) operating on Dropbox, Discord, Gmail, and OneNote, using 51 packet captures (3 baselines, 6 automated browser tests and 6 framework tests per service). Across four detection tiers, Reputation-based detection failed to identify any C2 channels; Beacon Detection was marginally viable when using clustering (2/4); Traffic Metadata was partially viable, with mixed results other than JA4 fingerprints (100% detection); and Traffic Patterns proved most viable, with both TLS session resumption near-zero (vs 22%+ for browser) and a 2.6x upload/download ratio gap (1.41 vs 0.55 means). Structural and behavioral indicators, such as TLS session resumption and JA4 fingerprinting, outperform reputation in detecting trusted service abuse.
algorithms: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN)
research_understanding.motivation: When adversary infrastructure resides within the trust boundary of a public cloud service (e.g., Microsoft, Google, Dropbox, Discord), reputation cannot discern malicious from legitimate traffic, creating a critical gap in network defense.
objectives: Assess four detection tiers (reputation, beacon detection, traffic metadata, traffic patterns) against C2 abuse of trusted services.
Evaluate structural and behavioral indicators (upload/download ratio, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, TLS metadata, connection duration/concurrency) against normal user traffic.
Develop and evaluate a proof-of-concept real-time detector using Zeek logs to detect C2 traffic over trusted services.
research_understanding.conclusions: Reputation-based detection and standard beacon timing analysis are ineffective against C2 operating over trusted public services. Behavioral and structural artifacts—especially upload/download ratio, JA4 baselining, TLS session resumption anomalies, and connection duration/persistence—enable high-confidence detection.
future_work: Evaluation of additional cloud services (e.g., computing, development, or enterprise collaboration platforms).
Testing official native desktop applications rather than solely web browser interfaces.
Longer capture durations (hours/days) and mixed-traffic scenarios.
Integration into native Zeek scripts or SIEM/IDS platforms with weighted scoring.
limitations: Only four specific services (Dropbox, Discord, Gmail, OneNote) and a single C2 framework per service were evaluated.
Slack and Microsoft Teams were not tested or evaluated.
Short capture duration (900 seconds) limits beacon periodicity detection.
Web browser automation via Selenium does not capture the full diversity of human user behavior or official desktop application behavior.
Framework modifications to capture SSLKEYLOGFILE altered TLS fingerprints (e.g., empty SNI behavior via BouncyCastle) for DBC2 and Callidus.
research_understanding.methodology: The study contrasts automated normal browser traffic (Control Flow using Selenium) against phased execution of C2 frameworks (Test Flow using Pexpect/wexpect across Enumeration, Beacon, Interact, and Exit phases) over a 900-second window. Packet captures were collected via tcpdump on a network tap, processed with tshark and Zeek, enriched with external metadata (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, RDAP, WHOIS, CT logs), classified into 8 traffic bins, and analyzed across four detection tiers.
research_understanding.preprocessing: Traffic capture filtering by client MAC address; artifact extraction using tshark and Zeek for IPs, DNS queries, TLS SNI, HTTP URLs, and JA3/JA4 fingerprints; enrichment via VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, RDAP, WHOIS, Certificate Transparency; rule-based classification into 8 categories.
research_understanding.problem_statement: The use of trusted public cloud services allows threat actors to subvert traditional reputation-based and beaconing detection mechanisms for Command and Control (C2), as malicious network traffic shares infrastructure and domains with reputable services.
research_understanding.experimental_setup: Test network composed of cloud services, a server network (192.168.2.1/24), a client network (192.168.1.1/24), and an L2 bridge tap collecting tcpdump traffic. Client machine (192.168.1.66) executed agents and automated browser flows; server (192.168.2.154) hosted C2 servers and Stage 2 listener.
research_questions: What network artifacts or indicators can be used to identify Command and Control (C2) when adversary infrastructure is within the trust boundary of a public service?
research_understanding.sufficiency_reason: The paper does not evaluate or mention detection rates for C2 traffic tunneled through Slack or Microsoft Teams; it exclusively investigates Dropbox (DBC2), Discord (DaaC2), Gmail (gdog), and OneNote (Callidus).

missing_information.why_needed: The user asked for detection rates specific to Slack and Microsoft Teams C2 traffic, but the study only evaluated Dropbox, Discord, Gmail, and OneNote.
missing_information.description: The study does not include experiments, captures, or detection rates for C2 traffic tunneled through Slack or Microsoft Teams.
missing_information.search_intent: Detection rate of C2 traffic tunneled through Slack or Microsoft Teams

explicit_assumptions: Adversaries use public cloud service APIs or interfaces to bypass traditional perimeter reputation defenses.
A baseline of normal enterprise operating system and browser traffic can be established for comparison.

ai_profile.summary: This study investigates how Command and Control (C2) frameworks abuse trusted services like Dropbox, Discord, Gmail, and OneNote by bypassing traditional reputation-based detection methods. The research compares normal user traffic against malicious activity using 51 packet captures to evaluate four detection tiers, finding that structural indicators such as JA4 fingerprints and TLS session resumption are significantly more effective than reputation or beacon detection. Ultimately, the paper argues that behavioral artifacts provide superior signals for identifying trusted service abuse compared to conventional network security indicators. The document details a research methodology for analyzing Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse using control flows and test frameworks like Pexpect. It describes a 900-second capture window divided into four phases (Enumeration, Beacon, Interact, Exit) executed across various services such as Discord, Dropbox, Gmail, and OneNote. The study involves collecting packet data via tcpdump from a configured network topology to enrich and classify artifacts using tools like tshark and Zeek. This document outlines limitations in a research study on trusted service abuse, including short test durations and reliance on web browser automation. It presents findings indicating that reputation-based detection is not viable for identifying command-and-control frameworks, while traffic patterns and upload/download ratios remain the most effective detection methods. This document analyzes network artifacts to detect malicious frameworks like Callidus and DaaC2, evaluating methods such as reputation checking, beacon detection, traffic metadata, and upload/download ratios. While reputation services like VirusTotal and AbuseIP DB showed limited success with few detections, traffic metadata analysis using JA3/JA4 signatures proved partially viable due to their stability despite the difficulty of maintaining baselines. The most viable method identified was analyzing traffic patterns, specifically the upload-to-download ratio, which clearly distinguished framework activity from normal service usage. The analysis reveals that Command-and-Control frameworks exhibit distinct network artifacts compared to browsers, including a lack of TLS session resumption and unique JA4 signatures. While domain reputation is ineffective for detection, indicators like upload-to-download ratios and connection duration patterns provide strong signals when combined with baseline data. The study concludes that standalone indicators such as JA4 fingerprinting can reliably identify frameworks without false positives. The study evaluates real-time detection methods for Command and Control (C2) frameworks abusing trusted services like Discord, Dropbox, Gmail, and OneNote using Zeek logs and Python scripts. While basic DNS analysis failed to reveal patterns, a tuned rule-based detector successfully identified all four tested frameworks with high confidence by analyzing indicators such as upload/download ratios and JA3/JA4 fingerprints. The research concludes that reputation-based detection is ineffective because these frameworks operate over trusted cloud providers without triggering known malicious indicators. The document details a research project analyzing network artifacts of trusted service abuse, specifically focusing on Command-and-Control (C&C) infrastructure using frameworks like JA4, DBC2, and gdog. It highlights the stability of JA4 fingerprints and the effectiveness of combining them with other indicators to detect malicious traffic without false positives. Additionally, it includes a command cross-walk table comparing various C2 tools and a declaration regarding the use of AI assistance in building test harnesses and analyzing data. The document details modifications to various Command and Control (C2) frameworks, including Discord, Dropbox, gdog, and Callidus, focusing on TLS decryption support and Python version updates. It presents reputation findings identifying malicious endpoints used for reconnaissance and dual-use purposes across services like Gmail, OneNote, and Discord. Additionally, the text outlines clustering results using K-Means and DBSCAN algorithms to classify network traffic as beacons, likely connections, or noise based on specific statistical thresholds. The document outlines network artifacts used to detect trusted service abuse, including derived sets from baseline indicator captures and specific trigger conditions for real-time detection. It lists vendor sources like Microsoft, Google, and Discord alongside community references such as v2fly and Certificate Transparency data. The text details technical thresholds for identifying anomalous traffic patterns, such as upload/download ratios, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, and connection duration metrics.
